title: Pompeii: The Last 24 Hours of a Roman City
youtube_title: Pompeii: The Last 24 Hours of a Roman City | Full Documentary
description:
In 79 AD, Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii under stone and ash in little more than a day. Using the eyewitness letters of Pliny the Younger and the latest archaeology, we follow the city hour by hour, from the first column of ash to the surge that ended it, and the rediscovery that brought it back.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #pompeii #vesuvius #ancientrome #documentary

beats.say: It is early afternoon, and a mountain has just torn itself open.
Above Vesuvius, a column of ash and stone is climbing kilometres into the sky.
About ten kilometres away, in the city of Pompeii, people stop in the street and look up.
Within hours, stones will fall from the sky. By the next morning, a cloud of burning gas will pour through the streets.
Some people will run. Some will stay. Many of those who stay will never leave.
And across the bay, a seventeen-year-old boy is watching it all. One day, he will write it down.
This is the story of the last day of Pompeii.
In 79 AD, Rome ruled every shore of the Mediterranean.
About two hundred kilometres south of the capital lay the Bay of Naples, a favourite playground of the Roman rich.
Around its curving shore sat busy towns: Naples, Herculaneum, Pompeii, and the great naval base at Misenum.
Pompeii stood near the mouth of the Sarno River. Goods came in by sea and went out along the roads.
It had been a Roman colony since 80 BC, when the general Sulla settled his veterans there after a war.
Before Rome took over, its people spoke a local language called Oscan. After that, Latin took its place.
Its people were a mix of free citizens, freed slaves and the enslaved.
No census survives. Historians think perhaps ten to twenty thousand people lived there.
It had temples, bathhouses, bakeries and bars.
It had an amphitheatre built around 70 BC, thought to be the oldest Roman amphitheatre still standing.
And its walls were covered in writing. Jokes, insults, love notes, and thousands of painted election notices.
Candidates for local office paid painters to put their names and promises up on the walls, like campaign posters.
It was a noisy, crowded, ordinary Roman town.
Above it all rose a green mountain, covered in vineyards and forest.
Most Romans had no idea it was a volcano.
The geographer Strabo had noticed that its summit looked scorched, and guessed there might once have been fire inside.
Nobody took that as a warning.
But the ground beneath the bay was about to send one.
On the fifth of February, in 62 AD, the ground under Campania began to shake.
Some sources put it a year later, in 63. The damage is not in doubt.
Buildings cracked and fell in Pompeii and Herculaneum.
The philosopher Seneca wrote about it. He reported a flock of six hundred sheep found dead, and blamed poisonous air.

show.label: HOUSE OF CAECILIUS IUCUNDUS
show.sub: A stone relief carved after the quake

beats.say: In one Pompeii house, the family of a banker named Caecilius Iucundus put up a stone relief of the disaster.
It shows the Temple of Jupiter and a city gate as the earth heaved.
Many scholars read it as a thank-you to the household gods, for letting the family survive.
Then Pompeii did what cities do. It rebuilt.

show.label: STILL REBUILDING
show.sub: years after the quake, repairs were unfinished

beats.say: Seventeen years later, the work was still not finished.
Skilled workers were scarce, and the rebuilding dragged on and on.
When the end came, parts of the city were still a building site.
Some volcanologists think the quake of 62 may have been an early sign of magma stirring below. That link is still debated.
Small tremors went on, too. In the days before the eruption, the young Pliny felt slight shocks.
He wrote that they were not particularly alarming, because they were common enough in Campania.
He was wrong. And soon the mountain would prove it.
Across the bay at Misenum, the commander of the Roman fleet was resting after lunch.
He was Pliny the Elder, a famous writer on nature, then in his fifties.
Staying with him was his nephew, Pliny the Younger, just seventeen years old.
At about the seventh hour, roughly one in the afternoon, the boy's mother pointed out a cloud of unusual size and shape.

show.text: In likeness and form it more closely resembled a pine-tree than anything else.
show.who: PLINY THE YOUNGER · LETTER 6.16 · TRANS. J. B. FIRTH

beats.say: Years later, the nephew described it for his friend, the historian Tacitus.
He meant the umbrella pine of Italy. A tall trunk, spreading out flat at the top.
Volcanologists still call eruptions like this one Plinian, after him.
The oldest surviving copies of his letter give the date as the twenty-fourth of August.
But in 2018, archaeologists in Pompeii found a line of charcoal writing on a wall.
It gave a date: the sixteenth day before the first of November. That is the seventeenth of October.
The note has no year. But charcoal fades fast, so many think it was written only days before the disaster.
Autumn fruit, heavy clothing and braziers found in the ruins point the same way.
Many scholars now favour the twenty-fourth of October. Others still defend August. The debate is not over.
Whatever the date, the column rose fast. Scientists estimate it reached somewhere between fifteen and thirty kilometres high.
The wind carried it south and east. At Misenum, the sky stayed clear. Over Pompeii, it began to fall.
Pliny the Elder ordered a fast ship made ready, to take a closer look.
Then a message came from a woman named Rectina. Her villa lay beneath the mountain, and she begged to be rescued.
The scholar became a rescuer. He launched the fleet's warships and steered straight for the danger.
Ash fell on the decks, hotter and thicker the closer they came, with pumice and blackened stones.
Debris from the mountain blocked the shore. The helmsman urged him to turn back.

show.text: Fortune favours the bold; try to reach Pomponianus.
show.who: PLINY THE YOUNGER · LETTER 6.16 · TRANS. J. B. FIRTH

beats.say: Pliny hesitated for a moment. Then he gave his answer.
Pomponianus was a friend at Stabiae, farther down the coast. Pliny sailed on.
He would never sail home.
In Pompeii, it was raining stone.
Not lava. Pumice. Light, grey-white stones full of air bubbles, falling hour after hour.
It filled the streets and courtyards. By the end, it lay close to three metres deep.
Each stone was light. The danger was the weight of millions of them, piling up on every roof.
This was the moment to run, and most people did.
Some took what they could carry. Some victims were later found with coins and jewellery.
Others stayed behind. Maybe they hoped to wait it out indoors. Maybe they could not leave.
It was a deadly gamble. As the pumice piled up, roofs began to give way under the weight.
Herculaneum, to the west of the mountain, got only a little of the falling pumice. Many of its people may have thought the worst had missed them.

show.label: KILLED IN THE PUMICE FALL
show.sub: of known victims, one 2003 study found

beats.say: One study found that about thirty-eight percent of the known victims died in this phase, most of them when roofs and walls fell in.
At Misenum, the young Pliny went back to his books, then bathed, ate, and slept badly.
That night, the earthquakes grew so strong that everything around him seemed about to topple.
His mother rushed into his room. They sat out in the courtyard, and he calmly read a volume of the historian Livy.
At Stabiae, Pliny the Elder had found his friend terrified, his baggage already loaded on a ship.
The wind was blowing onshore. Nobody could sail out.
To calm everyone, Pliny bathed, ate dinner in good spirits, and went to bed.
He slept so deeply that the servants could hear his heavy breathing through the door.
Outside, the courtyard filled with ash and pumice. If he had stayed much longer, he would have been trapped inside.
They woke him. The buildings were rocking with earthquakes.
So they tied pillows to their heads against the falling stones, and walked to the shore by torchlight.
Elsewhere, morning had come. At Stabiae, it was darker than any night.
Some time after midnight, the great column over Vesuvius had begun to collapse.
What came down the mountain was not rain. It was fire that could run.
When an eruption column grows too heavy to hold itself up, it falls.
A flood of hot gas, ash and rock pours down the slopes.
Scientists call it a pyroclastic surge. It moves faster than anyone can run, at hundreds of degrees.
Herculaneum, closer to the mountain, was hit first, in the dark hours of the night.
Crowds of people had packed into the stone boathouses on the beach, hoping for rescue by sea.
In the 1980s, archaeologists found the remains of nearly three hundred people there and on the old shoreline.
Many scientists think the heat killed them almost instantly.
The surges kept coming. One classic study counts six of them.
Early in the morning, one of them reached Pompeii.
For anyone still in the city, there was no escape.
People died in streets and gardens, in doorways and in rooms where they had sheltered.
The ash buried them where they fell.
At Stabiae, flames and the smell of sulphur scattered Pliny's party.
Leaning on two slaves, Pliny stood up, and fell again.
His nephew believed the thick fumes had choked him.
When daylight returned, his body was found untouched, looking more like a man asleep than a dead one.
Across the bay, Misenum was shaking too. The young Pliny and his mother fled the town with a panicked crowd.
The sea pulled back from the shore, leaving sea creatures stranded on the sand.
Then the black cloud came down over the water and hid the island of Capri.
His mother begged him to leave her and save himself. He took her hand, and refused.
Darkness caught them on the road.

show.text: You could hear the wailing of women, the screams of little children, and the shouts of men.
show.who: PLINY THE YOUNGER · LETTER 6.20 · TRANS. J. B. FIRTH

beats.say: People called out in the dark, trying to find their families by their voices alone.

show.text: Now there were no more gods, and this night would last for ever, and the end of all the world.
show.who: PLINY THE YOUNGER · LETTER 6.20 · TRANS. J. B. FIRTH

beats.say: Many, he wrote, believed the gods were gone and the world was ending.
But the night did end. The sun came out, dim and blood-red, over a land buried in ash like snow.
Pompeii was gone. And for more than sixteen hundred years, it would stay lost.

show.label: BODIES FOUND IN POMPEII
show.sub: The full death toll is unknown

beats.say: No one knows how many people died.
More than eleven hundred bodies have been found in Pompeii so far. Some estimates put the city's dead at around two thousand.
The toll across the whole bay is anyone's guess.

show.label: REDISCOVERY
show.sub: Digging begins at a site called La Civita

beats.say: In 1748, workers for the King of Naples began digging at a place the locals called La Civita.
In 1763, they found an inscription naming the people of Pompeii. The lost city had its name back.
The early digs were mostly hunts for treasure.
Nearby Herculaneum had been tunnelled for ten years already, from 1738, for its statues and marble.
Then, in 1863, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli tried something new.
The victims' bodies had decayed inside the hardened ash, leaving hollows in their exact shape.
Fiorelli poured liquid plaster into those hollows. When the ash was chipped away, people appeared.
Curled up. Arms raised. Some lying side by side.
Since then, a little over a hundred casts have been made.

show.label: DNA STUDY · 2024
show.sub: Ancient DNA from the plaster casts

beats.say: In 2024, scientists tested DNA from some of the casts, and found surprises.
An adult holding a child, long called a mother, was a man, and not related to the child.
The digging goes on. In 2023, archaeologists uncovered a bakery with barred windows.
Inside, enslaved workers and blindfolded donkeys had turned the heavy millstones.
And about a third of the city is still buried.
The boy who survived grew up to be a senator. About twenty-five years later, he wrote down what he saw.
His letters are the only eyewitness account of the eruption to survive.
Pompeii was not frozen in one moment. It was a city of people who ran, stayed, prayed, and tried to save each other.
And Vesuvius is still there, still active, above the bay.
